title: How Much Do Contact Lenses Cost in 2026?
summary: How much do contacts cost? An annual supply of standard soft lenses runs about $120 to $1,000. See prices by lens type, exam and fitting fees, and tips.
body_markdown:
If you wear contacts or you're thinking about switching from wearing glasses, it helps to know what you'll actually pay. For standard soft contact lenses in both eyes, an annual supply typically costs about **$120 to $1,000** , depending mostly on how often you replace them. Daily disposables sit at the top of that range and monthly contacts at the bottom. Exams, fittings, and cleaning supplies add to the total.


This guide breaks down the price of contact lenses by type, explains what drives the cost, and shows how to estimate your own yearly spending.


## Quick Answer: How Much Do Contacts Cost?

Real prices vary based on brand, retailer, and rebates, so use these ranges as a starting point and check current prices for the exact lens your eye doctor prescribes.


You need a valid prescription to buy contact lenses in the U.S. Under the FTC's[Contact Lens Rule](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/buying-prescription-glasses-or-contact-lenses-your-rights) , your eye doctor must give you a copy of your contact lens prescription after a fitting, and you can buy your lenses from any seller, in a store or online.


## What Drives the Cost of Contact Lenses?


A few predictable factors determine how much contact lenses cost.


**Your prescription.** Correcting simple nearsightedness (myopia) or farsightedness is the least expensive. Astigmatism (toric lenses) and presbyopia (multifocal lenses) require more complex lens designs, which raise the price per box.


**Replacement schedule.** Daily disposables cost the most per year because you use a fresh pair every day, but you don't need cleaning solution or cases. Two-week and monthly disposables cost less in lenses but need solution and a case.


**Lens material.** Silicone hydrogel lenses, which let more oxygen reach the eye, usually cost more than basic hydrogel lenses. Rigid gas permeable lenses are often custom-made.


**Brand and retailer.** Prices for the same lens can vary between your optometrist's office, big-box stores, and online retailers, depending on overhead, bulk discounts, and manufacturer rebates. Switching to a different brand can also change the price.


Other factors add to the cost of contacts: lens care solution, cases, backup[glasses](https://www.withflex.com/blog/can-you-use-hsa-fsa-for-glasses) or other eyewear, and regular eye exams and fittings, which are separate from the lenses themselves.


## Soft Contact Lenses by Replacement Schedule


Soft contact lenses are the most common type and come in daily, two-week, and monthly versions. These are all daily wear contacts, meaning you take them out before you sleep.


**Daily disposable lenses.** You put in a fresh pair each morning and throw them away at night. A 90-lens box costs about $50 to $122, and full-time wear in both eyes takes about 8 boxes a year. Dailies skip cleaning solution and cases, which is convenient but doesn't fully offset their higher lens cost.


**Two-week lenses.** A 6-lens box typically costs $25 to $35. Worn as directed, you'll need about 9 boxes a year for both eyes, plus cleaning solution.


**Monthly contacts.** A 6-lens box of monthly disposables costs about $30 to $50, and full-time wear in both eyes takes 4 boxes a year. Monthly contacts are usually the least expensive soft option, even after adding solution and a lens case.


## Rigid Gas Permeable (RGP) Lenses: Upfront vs. Long-Term Cost


Rigid gas permeable lenses cost more per lens, about $35 to $95 each according to Vision Center, but one pair can last a year or longer with proper care. That durability can make them competitive with soft contact lenses on a yearly basis.


Your eye doctor will help you decide whether RGP or soft lenses make more sense. RGPs are often recommended for high astigmatism or corneal conditions like keratoconus, and many people say they give clearer vision. Fitting them usually takes more time, so fitting fees tend to be higher.


## Toric, Multifocal, Extended Wear, and Specialty Lenses


Toric lenses correct astigmatism and cost more per box than standard lenses with the same replacement schedule. Multifocal lenses, which correct near and distance vision for people with presbyopia, are among the most expensive soft lenses, especially as dailies.


Extended wear contacts are approved to be worn overnight for a set number of days. They're priced similarly to other monthly contacts, but talk with your eye doctor or ophthalmologist before sleeping in any contact lens, because overnight wear raises the risk of eye infections.


Specialty lenses such as scleral lenses for keratoconus and orthokeratology lenses (worn overnight to reshape the cornea) are usually custom-made and sit in the highest price tier.


## Contact Lens Exams and Fittings


Lens prices are only part of the answer to "how much do contacts cost." A contact lens exam includes a fitting that a routine eye exam doesn't, and it's billed separately.


- An eye exam can cost about $40 to $240 without insurance, according to Vision Center.
- A contact lens fitting adds about $25 to $250. Standard soft lens fittings tend to cost less, while toric, multifocal, and RGP fittings cost more.
- Fittings usually include corneal measurements, trial lenses, and one or two follow-up visits.


Vision insurance often covers part of the exam and gives an allowance for contact lenses, but the amount varies by plan. Your contact lens prescription typically needs to be renewed regularly, so plan for a recurring exam.


## Where to Buy Contact Lenses and How Pricing Differs


You can order contacts from several kinds of sellers, as long as you have a valid prescription.


**Your optometrist's office.** You get personalized service and easy follow-up, but prices may be higher. Some offices bundle the exam and lenses.


**Big-box stores and pharmacies.** These often stock popular brands at competitive prices, especially standard soft contact lenses. Selection for specialty lenses may be limited.


**When you buy contact lenses online.** Online retailers and websites let you compare prices across brands, buy an annual supply, and set up subscriptions. Under the FTC rule, if you don't send a copy of your prescription, the seller must verify it with your eye doctor before shipping.


Buying an annual supply at once can unlock manufacturer rebates and bulk discounts, which is one of the easiest ways to save money. Look for rebates and shipping promotions when comparing retailers, and ask whether your vision insurance gives a larger allowance if you order a full year at once.


## How to Estimate Your Total Yearly Cost


To answer "how much do contacts cost per year" for your own situation, look beyond the per-box price:


- Count the boxes you'll need for both eyes in a year, based on your replacement schedule.
- Add cleaning solution and cases if you don't wear dailies. A bottle of solution costs about $5 to $20.
- Add the cost of your eye exam, fitting, and backup glasses.


Compare at least two different types side by side. For example, a full-time wearer switching from daily disposables to monthly contacts can cut lens costs by several hundred dollars a year, even after paying for solution. If you wear contacts only part-time, dailies can be cost-effective because you only open what you use.


## Paying for Contacts: Insurance, Cash, and HSAs or FSAs


Vision insurance is the most common way to lower what you pay. If you don't have vision coverage, ask your eye doctor and retailers about cash prices and rebates on an annual supply.


[IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) lists contact lenses needed for medical reasons as a medical expense, along with the saline solution and enzyme cleaner needed to use them. Whether you can use an HSA or FSA for a particular purchase depends on your plan's rules, so check with your plan administrator. Our guide to[HSAs and FSAs](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) explains how the two accounts work.


## How to Choose Lenses That Fit Your Budget


Consult your eye doctor about whether daily, two-week, or monthly contacts make the most sense for how often you wear contacts and how sensitive your eyes are, especially if you have dry eyes. Ask for a comparison of yearly costs for at least two options. If you need toric or multifocal correction, ask whether a different brand could offer similar comfort at a lower price.


Keep your prescription current, don't wear lenses longer than their replacement schedule (it can lead to eye infections that cost far more), and keep a pair of backup glasses for days you give your eyes a break.
